newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Price war undermines Peugeot profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Price war undermines Peugeot profit.

text.p: Carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen said on Thursday its profit was cut by more than half last year by a price war raging through the French market.
Chairman Jacques Calvet said the outlook for this year was also grim with no sign of a letup in the competitive discounting that has eroded the industry's profits in Europe.
The group slashed its dividend after reporting 1996 net attributable profit of 734 million francs ($126 million), down 57 percent from 1.70 billion for 1995 and far below analysts' expectations.
Its shares tumbled 5.3 percent to 605 francs by early afternoon.

"The price war was the main feature of 1996. European carmakers all reported sharp earnings declines. Renault and Ford Europe posted losses, PSA Peugeot Citroen's profit was cut by more than half and Fiat's operating margin fell by two-thirds," Calvet told a news conference.
Last month Renault reported its first loss in 10 years -- a deficit of 5.25 billion francs including 3.9 billion in restructuring charges.
The fierce competition among carmakers undercut the benefits of a 10.5 percent jump last year in French car sales, fuelled by a state rebate programme in effect during the first nine months of 1996.
The Peugeot group's operating profit fell to 1.675 billion francs from 3.751 billion in 1995, even though sales rose to 172.7 billion francs from 164.2 billion.
It cut its net dividend to three francs per share from five.

Calvet said he did not expect price pressures to abate this year. The situation is exacerbated by weak demand in the French market, which is taking longer than expected to bounce back from a post-rebate slump.
"We knew there would be a backlash after the rebates ended but we didn't think it would be this bad or last this long," he said.
The group has revised its market forecast and expects car sales to fall 11.5 percent in France this year. It had previously forecast a 10 percent drop in the market.
Asked if the company would be profitable during 1997 amid such tough conditions, Calvet said that was the objective. "Are we 100 percent sure? The answer is no," he said.
"What is certain is that I won't present the results," he said, confirming plans to retire. Calvet, who turns 66 this year, must step down in the autumn under company bylaws.
He did not say who would succeed him but reinforced speculation that it would be car operations director Jean-Martin Folz by announcing Folz's appointment to the management board.

Unlike rival Renault, which announced big job cuts and a restructuring of its car assembly operations in light of its losses, the Peugeot group did not announce major cost-cutting measures. Calvet said the company would accelerate efforts to produce more successful models for less.
Analysts do not expect significant changes to be announced until the new management takes over.

The Peugeot group produces cars at a lower cost than Renault but, like its domestic rival, is overly dependent on the European market, which has become the global battleground as protective barriers fall away.
The Peugeot group sold 87 percent of its cars and light commercial vehicles in western Europe last year.

Calvet renewed his call to prolong European import quotas for Japanese car producers beyond the year 2000 and said Europe should fight against unfair south Korean trade practices. ($ = 5.810 French Francs)
